title: Koosa mahshi
subtitle: Levantine stuffed courgettes in tomato sauce
excerpt: Koosa mahshi are small courgettes hollowed out and stuffed with a spiced rice and lamb mixture, then braised slowly in a gently spiced tomato sauce until tender throughout. They are one of the most time-consuming and most rewarding dishes in the Levantine kitchen.
sourceNotes: Mahshi (stuffed vegetables) is a broad family of dishes across the Levant, Egypt, and Turkey. Koosa (courgette) is one of the most popular vehicles. The dish appears in Lebanese, Syrian, Palestinian, Egyptian, and Turkish cooking with regional variations.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Stuffed courgettes can be prepared and refrigerated uncooked for up to a day. Cook fresh.

content.text: Koosa mahshi requires patience at the preparation stage. Each courgette is hollowed using a special corer or a small, thin knife, leaving walls about 5 mm thick. The stuffing goes in raw, with room for the rice to expand during cooking. Then the whole pot braises, and the courgette flesh becomes very tender around the savoury filling.
The effort at the hollowing stage pays off in the eating. Each courgette arrives at the table intact, with its own pocket of seasoned rice and lamb, soaked in tomato broth.

Koosa courgettes are small; use the smallest courgettes you can find, ideally around 12 to 15 cm long and no thicker than a large sausage. Standard supermarket courgettes work but are slightly harder to hollow without breaking.

Trim the stalk end of each courgette but leave the tip intact. Use an apple corer or the thin end of a vegetable peeler to hollow out the core, leaving walls about 5 mm thick all around. Do not puncture the tip. Rinse and set aside. Reserve the scooped flesh for another use.

Mix together the rice, lamb mince, diced onion, allspice, cinnamon, salt, pepper, and butter. The mixture will look quite loose; this is correct. Use a teaspoon to fill each courgette to about two-thirds full; the rice will expand as it cooks and needs room.

Mix the passata, water, garlic, salt, and lemon juice in a large, wide saucepan. Arrange the stuffed courgettes in a single layer in the pot, opening-end up. The sauce should come halfway up the courgettes. Bring to a gentle boil, reduce to a low simmer, cover, and cook for 50 to 60 minutes until the courgettes are very tender and the rice is fully cooked. Add a little hot water during cooking if the sauce reduces too much.

rows.cause: Stuffed too full or heat too high
rows.fix: Fill to two-thirds only; the rice must have room. Keep at a gentle simmer, not a rolling boil.

rows.cause: Heat too low or not enough liquid
rows.fix: Add 100 ml of hot water around the courgettes and continue for 15 more minutes covered.

rows.symptom: Courgette walls too thin and breaking
rows.cause: Corer cut too close to the skin
rows.fix: Leave 5 mm of flesh all around. Use a long, thin tool and work slowly from the open end.

content.text: For a vegetarian version, replace the lamb with a mixture of mushroom, finely diced onion, and toasted pine nuts. Some versions cook the courgettes in a yoghurt sauce rather than tomato; this gives a completely different, more delicate flavour.
The stuffed but uncooked courgettes can be covered and refrigerated for up to a day. Cook from refrigerated; add 10 minutes to the braising time.

Stuffed vegetables are central to cooking across the Levant. Koosa mahshi appears in Lebanese, Syrian, Palestinian, and Egyptian home kitchens, each with minor variations in spicing and sauce. It is weekend food, made when time allows, and is one of the dishes that marks a cook who has the patience to do it properly.
